Thank you for the briefing. The panel has noted all six points. A few things already stand out that we'll keep in mind as you bring plans forward:

**Velvet Pika (Finance)** flags the 60% video-appointment rate and the uncertain funding for the two fixed-term nurses as live budget pressures — any plan that assumes current staffing or income levels will need to account for both.

**Ripple Kite (Operations)** notes the vaccine handover cap of 50 doses a day runs until 12 January, the two-nurse capacity cliff at year-end, and the three-month landlord lead time — all of which will constrain anything time-sensitive.

**Crimson Crow (Patients)** wants to keep the 45%-over-70 cohort front of mind, particularly their limited smartphone use, whenever digital or remote options come up. And that 25-minute phone wait is already a pain point we shouldn't make worse.

**Lunar Stoat (Chair)** confirms the panel has a clear picture of the constraints. We're ready to review plans as you bring them. Looking forward to working with you.

**DECISION MEMO**
**Brookside Health Centre — Cleaning Contractor Decision**
*Prepared by the Advisory Panel | 13 October 2036*

---

**Recommendation**

**Option B — retain the current contractor**, while opening a structured tender process to test whether better value is available.

---

**Problems with the plan**

The plan contains a material arithmetic error. Spotless Partners' quote is $3,400 per month, but clinical-waste collection adds $650, bringing the true like-for-like cost to $4,050. The real monthly saving is $150, not $800 — $1,800 per year, not $9,600. That changes the entire financial case.

Beyond the numbers, the due diligence is inadequate for a clinical setting. A single phone call is not a sufficient basis for selecting a contractor who will operate in a regulated healthcare environment. Key unknowns include: whether Spotless staff hold infection-control certificates, what their clinical-waste handling procedures are, their insurance and liability position, references from comparable clients, and their contractual terms on notice and performance.

A 1 November start date gives fewer than three weeks to verify compliance, brief staff, and manage transition. That is an unsafe timeline in a clinical environment where a lapse in infection control carries regulatory and patient-safety consequences.

Option C is dismissed too quickly. The "too cheap to be realistic" rationale is not an analysis. Direct employment at $2,900 per month warrants proper examination, including on-costs, management overhead, and whether infection-control training can be provided in-house.

---

**Options weighed**

| Option | Monthly cost | Key risk |
|---|---|---|
| A — Spotless Partners | $4,050 | Unverified compliance; rushed transition |
| B — Current contractor | $4,200 | Slightly higher cost; known and compliant |
| C — Own cleaners | $2,900+ | On-costs and management burden unclear |

---

**What would change this recommendation**

Switch to Option A if Spotless Partners can demonstrate certified infection-control training, provide satisfactory references from clinical clients, confirm compliant clinical-waste procedures, and allow a transition period of at least six to eight weeks. Switch to Option C if a full cost analysis — including employer on-costs, training, cover for absence, and management time — confirms it delivers genuine savings without compliance gaps.

A formal tender across all three options, run properly, remains the recommended next step.

**DECISION MEMO**
**Brookside Health Centre — Appointment Booking**
**Date: 20 October 2036**

---

**Recommendation**

**Option B** — launch the app alongside a call-back service on the phone line at peak times.

---

**Problems with the plan**

The plan has four significant weaknesses.

**Unrealistic take-up assumption.** The 85% figure comes from a university health service whose patients are predominantly young, digitally confident students. A community clinic serves a much broader demographic, including older adults and people with limited smartphone access or digital literacy. Expecting equivalent take-up within one month is not credible.

**Unresolved system integration.** The app supplier has not confirmed the link to the patient-records system. Launching on 1 December without a working integration risks booking errors, duplicate records, and patient safety incidents. A fixed launch date against an unconfirmed technical dependency is a serious operational risk.

**Inadequate patient transition support.** A $2,000 poster-and-leaflet budget is thin for a change that affects every patient. Patients who cannot or do not use the app by 1 December will have no way to book at all under Option A. That is an access and safety issue, not merely an inconvenience.

**Hidden costs.** The $1,200 monthly subscription is only part of the picture. Staff training, IT support, and any remediation of integration failures are not budgeted. If the integration requires paid development work, costs could rise sharply before launch.

---

**Options weighed**

**Option A** removes phone booking entirely before patient take-up is proven and before the system link is confirmed. The risk of excluding vulnerable patients is unacceptably high.

**Option B** keeps a call-back safety net on the phones during peak hours, reducing the 8am rush without cutting off patients who cannot use the app. It allows take-up to build at a realistic pace and buys time to confirm the system integration properly.

**Option C** adds reception staff costs permanently and does nothing to modernise booking. It solves the symptom, not the problem.

---

**What would change this recommendation**

Move to Option A only if: the system integration is confirmed and tested before launch; an independent take-up assessment for a community-clinic demographic supports the 85% figure; and a funded support programme for digitally excluded patients is in place. If costs prove unaffordable, Option C remains the fallback.

# Decision Memo – Flu Vaccination Drive 2036

## Recommendation

**Option B – run smaller daytime clinics spread over eight weeks.**

---

## Problems with the plan

**Capacity shortfall.** Five nurses each vaccinating 12 patients per hour across three hours yields 180 vaccinations per clinic, not 80 – so throughput is not the binding constraint. The binding constraint is **recording time**. At 3 minutes per patient, 80 vaccinations generate 240 minutes of post-clinic admin per nurse – far exceeding the three-hour paid window. Record-keeping is not costed in the overtime budget, creating either unpaid work or incomplete records, both of which are unacceptable.

**No-show risk.** With a 15% historical no-show rate, roughly 180 of the 1,200 booked patients will not attend. The plan makes no provision for standby patients or rebooking, so the drive will likely deliver around 1,020 vaccinations, not 1,200.

**Staff fatigue.** Fifteen evening clinics over five weeks, on top of normal daytime duties, is a heavy burden on all five nurses. Sustained overtime at this intensity raises wellbeing and retention risks.

**Seasonal timing.** A drive ending 12 December is already late in the flu season; any slippage pushes it later still. Option C (January) would be materially worse on clinical grounds.

---

## Options weighed

| | A – As planned | B – Daytime, 8 weeks | C – January |
|---|---|---|---|
| Financially sound | No – admin uncosted | Yes – regular hours | Partial |
| Operationally feasible | No – admin overrun | Yes | Yes |
| Good for patients | Moderate – late, some missed | Better – accessible slots | Poor – too late |
| Hits 1,200 target | Unlikely (~1,020) | Achievable with standby list | Uncertain |

Option C is ruled out: January vaccination offers significantly reduced clinical benefit.

---

## What would change this recommendation

- If the overtime budget were extended to cover post-clinic admin time in full, and a standby patient list were added to absorb no-shows, Option A becomes viable.
- If daytime capacity is genuinely unavailable for eight weeks (e.g. room or staff conflicts), a hybrid – fewer evening clinics with explicit admin time built in – should be modelled before defaulting to Option A.

**DECISION MEMO — BROOKSIDE HEALTH CENTRE**
*Second Treatment Room / Capacity Expansion*
*Issued: 3 November 2036*

---

## Recommendation

**Option B — keep one treatment room and open two evenings a week from January, staffed by the existing nursing team.**

---

## Problems with the plan

**Storage is the critical flaw.** Corridor cupboards holding one-third of current stock is not a minor inconvenience — it creates a genuine clinical risk. Medical supplies need secure, accessible, temperature-appropriate storage. A shortfall here affects every patient seen, not just the additional 20%.

**Staffing headroom is unclear.** The plan assumes five nurses absorb a 20% appointment increase within existing contracted hours. No evidence is provided that this headroom exists. If nurses are already running close to capacity, the new room adds stress without adding staff, raising both safety and retention concerns.

**$30,000 capital spend is significant.** The plan offers no payback analysis, no funding source, and no contingency. If conversion overruns or the throughput gain is not realised, the clinic carries the cost with no recovery mechanism.

**December build disrupts December operations.** Construction starting 1 December hits the clinic during a typically high-demand winter period.

---

## Options weighed

**Option A (convert as planned):** Offers the largest long-term capacity gain but carries three simultaneous risks — unresolved storage, unverified staffing headroom, and a $30,000 outlay with no payback case. Too many unknowns to proceed now.

**Option B (evening sessions):** Delivers capacity increase from January with no capital spend and no storage disruption. The staffing ask is real — evening work requires willing nurses and appropriate compensation — but it is a contained, reversible commitment. It also tests whether demand genuinely supports expansion before committing $30,000.

**Option C (delay conversion):** Sensible only if used productively. Delaying without a plan to resolve storage and staffing analysis simply defers the same problems.

---

## What would change this recommendation

Return to Option A if the clinic can demonstrate: (1) a compliant storage solution before building work begins; (2) confirmed nursing capacity or a funded staffing uplift; and (3) a simple payback analysis showing how the $30,000 is recovered. Option C becomes preferable to B if evening staffing proves unworkable with the current team.

# Panel Closing Responses

---

**Lunar Stoat (Chair):** These are good consolidating questions, but I have to be straightforward with all four answers: we don't have confident recall of the specifics from earlier discussions sufficient to answer these accurately. Let me be transparent about what that means for each one.

---

**1. Daily jab capacity — now and when it changes**

**Ripple Kite (Operations):** I don't have a reliable figure in memory for your current daily vaccination throughput, nor a confirmed date when that changes — for example due to a staff rota shift, a room coming in or out of use, or a seasonal programme ending. You'll need to pull that from your scheduling records. I wouldn't want to quote a number and have you plan around it incorrectly.

---

**2. Payment for remote/screen consultations**

**Velvet Pika (Finance):** The reimbursement structure for remote consultations wasn't something we pinned down with enough precision for me to state it confidently. Whether that's a flat fee, a reduced tariff, or parity with face-to-face under your current contract — I'd rather you check your commissioner or NHS contract terms directly than rely on my recall here.

---

**3. Clinical team strength after New Year**

**Ripple Kite (Operations):** We don't have confirmed information in memory about any departures, retirements, or contract changes affecting your doctors or nurses beyond January. If there's something known internally — a planned leave, a fixed-term contract ending — that needs to come from your own HR records.

---

**4. Room change approvals and timescales**

**Ripple Kite / Lunar Stoat:** Similarly, the specific approval chain — whether that's a landlord, a primary care network lead, an ICB estates team, or a CQC notification — and the associated lead times weren't established in our discussions with enough detail to state reliably.

---

**Lunar Stoat (Chair) — Summary:**

We'd rather give you four honest "we don't know" answers than four confident wrong ones. These are exactly the factual baselines you'd want nailed down before implementing any of the plans we've discussed. We'd recommend compiling them into a short pre-implementation checklist and getting confirmed answers from your scheduler, your contract, your HR lead, and your estates or landlord contact respectively.
